utterance: G'day Graham. I'm glad your wife convinced you to come in. Before we do anything, I want to understand exactly what's going on. Can you describe this "indigestion" for me — where do you feel it, and what does it actually feel like?
reply: It is like a heaviness. Like indigestion but... heavier. Sort of a weight sitting on my chest. Right in the middle, behind the breastbone. Bit up into the throat. About seven this morning. Came on over a few minutes. It has been going the whole time, near enough an hour and a half, and it is still there now. Now you mention it, my jaw is a bit achy, and my left arm feels heavy. Not my back.

awards.label: Whether the discomfort spreads or travels anywhere (arms, jaw, neck, back)

utterance: That heaviness behind the breastbone, going into your jaw and left arm — I need to take that seriously. A few quick questions. What were you doing when it came on — resting or exerting yourself? And have you felt sweaty, sick in the stomach, short of breath, or lightheaded along with it? Ever had anything like this before, even a milder version?
reply: I was just sitting having a cuppa, reading the paper. I have been sweating like anything, thought it was just hot, and feel a bit sick, though I haven't vomited. I am a bit short of breath and it is hard to get a proper breath in, and I felt a bit light-headed getting out of the car, but I didn't pass out. This past week I have had a bit of a tightness going up ladders, but it goes away if I stop, and I just put it down to being unfit, though it has been happening more.

awards.label: Activity at the moment today's pain began
Red flag: Sweating or clamminess with the pain
Red flag: Dizziness, light-headedness or fainting
Red flag: Had this chest pain before, e.g. on stairs or exertion

result: Sinus bradycardia 54/min. ST elevation 2–3 mm in II, III and aVF. Reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No LBBB.
No ST elevation in V4R. No evidence of right ventricular involvement.

finding: Heart sounds dual, soft S4. No murmur. No rub.

utterance:
Graham, I want to be straight with you: this isn't indigestion. Your heart tracing shows you are having a heart attack right now — a blocked artery on the underside of your heart. That heavy feeling, the sweating, the jaw and arm ache — that's your heart.

Here's what I've done and what happens next. I've given you an aspirin tablet to chew — it thins the blood and helps stop the clot getting bigger. I've also sprayed a medicine called glyceryl trinitrate under your tongue, which opens up the blood vessels; it can give you a flushed feeling or a headache, and it should ease the pressure. Your lungs are clear and your blood pressure is holding up, which is good.

I've called an ambulance — it's on its way. You must not drive yourself. At hospital they can open that blocked artery, usually with a balloon and a small stent, and the sooner that happens the more heart muscle we save. Coming in when you did was exactly the right thing — your wife may well have saved your life.

While we wait: stay seated, try to stay calm, and tell me immediately if the pain gets worse, you feel faint, or more sweaty. If the heaviness hasn't eased in five minutes, I'll give you another spray. Do you have someone I should call — your wife?
reply: An ambulance? Hang on, Doc, can't I just drive myself? My ute is right out the front and I've got a job I need to finish this morning. You better call my missus, I suppose.

utterance:
No, mate — driving is not negotiable. Right now the lower part of your heart is being starved of blood, and that can trigger a dangerous, even fatal, heart rhythm without warning. If that happened behind the wheel, you could kill yourself and someone else on the road. In the ambulance the crew monitors your heart, can treat you on the way, and takes you straight to the right team — it's genuinely the fastest way to get the artery opened.

I understand the job is waiting — you're self-employed and that's stressful. But no tap or hot water system is worth dying over. I'll get our receptionist to call your wife right now so she can meet you at the hospital, and she can sort the job with your client.

How's that heaviness now, a few minutes after the spray — better, worse, or the same?
reply: I don't know. Maybe a six? It is more heavy than sore.

utterance:
Good — your abdomen is soft with no tenderness, so this is all coming from your heart, as the tracing showed. The second spray is in. The ambulance will be here any minute now; I'll hand over to the crew with your tracing and what I've given you — two sprays of glyceryl trinitrate and the aspirin. They'll take you to the cardiac team, who'll most likely take you straight to the cath lab to open that artery with a stent.

Reception is calling your wife now, so she can meet you at the hospital and help sort this morning's job. You've done everything right by coming in early — that gives you the best chance of a good recovery. Once this is behind you, we'll talk properly about the smoking, because quitting is the single best thing you can do for your heart from here. You're in good hands, Graham.
reply: I still reckon it's just my stomach, but if you and the missus say so, I suppose I will stay put.
